kind: A screen on the laptop's GPU, one seed, by slope over data: whether a stack that trains with output spikes of 1/16 bit turns the pulses its output no longer fires into bits, and whether it keeps its score when the budget is cut by what the output saves. Recorded before any run.
why: On trained weights an output spike can stand for 1/16 bit in place of 1/128 at a cost of 0.00004 bits per byte, and the stack then fires a third fewer pulses on the test bed and a fifth fewer at full size (output_step_on_trained_weights.json). That is a saving of energy. A stack that trains with coarse output spikes at the old budget has those pulses for its reads and cells: 55% more for its other populations on the test bed, 27% more at full size. The price of the pulse budget states what a pulse is worth to the loss: at the end of the base runs the whole budget's worth of pulses weighs 0.020 nats a byte at 6,000 updates and 0.0045 at 24,000 (rd-base-6k-s3, rd-base-24k-s3). If the price is right, the freed third of the budget is worth little late in training. This screen measures it.

arms.out8: --output-step 8: one output spike stands for 8 fine steps (1/16 bit); budget 113,000 as the base, so the other populations may fire what the output no longer does
arms.out8-b75: --output-step 8 --pulse-budget 75000: the budget cut by what the coarse output saves on the base's trained weights (112,659 to 74,787 pulses a byte at 24,000 updates), so the other populations fire about what they fire in the base: the saving as a way to train. At 6,000 updates the base's output fires fewer pulses, so there the arm's other populations get about 4,000 a byte fewer than the base's.

base: rd-base-6k-s3 and rd-base-24k-s3 (the delayed test bed at 1.2e-3, seed 20003, budget 113,000, fine output spikes, on the laptop: 1.628291 and 1.482439)
training: the delayed test bed's recipe at peak rate 1.2e-3, warmup 300, cosine over the run, 6,000 and 24,000 updates, seed 20003, on the laptop's GPU one run at a time after the queue's earlier runs; code: a frozen copy of the commit that records this screen; 5,249,060 parameters, as the base: the step adds no synapse
measure: experiments/eval_stream.py on the first 2,000,000 validation bytes as 16 unbroken streams, lead 8,192, averaged weights, bits kept, each arm scored with the output step it trained with and paired with the base of its length (experiments/compare_stream_scores.py); experiments/gap_by_piece.py (near 240, far 8,192); experiments/gate_state.py for the pulses a byte by population on the first 65,536 validation bytes, which shows where the freed pulses go; the price of the budget along training
prediction: From the price alone, to first order: out8 leads the base by about 0.009 bits per byte at 6,000 updates (0.020 nats for the whole budget times the 30% of it that the output frees) and by about 0.002 at 24,000 (0.0045 nats times 34%). out8-b75 is level with the base at both lengths. A lead at 24,000 updates well above 0.002 would mean that pulses are worth more along the way than the price at the end says.
reading: A screen with one seed. Arms that share a seed and change nothing that matters have differed by 0.001 to 0.004 (the nulls of gated_cells_with_data and noisy_thresholds_with_data). out8 earns two seeds on the server at both lengths and an arm with --output-step 8 in the next full-size pilot if it leads the base by at least 0.010 at 24,000 updates, or by at least 0.005 there with a lead no smaller than at 6,000 updates. Otherwise the coarse output stays what output_step_on_trained_weights.json showed, a saving of energy at no cost in bits, and is reported only. out8-b75 shows that the saving also holds as a way to train if it is within 0.004 of the base at 24,000 updates; if it trails by more, the saving is stated for trained weights alone. Recorded either way: both arms at both lengths, the split by context, the pulses by population and the price along training.
seen_before_recording: output_step_on_trained_weights.json (cd72ec3): the measurement on weights that trained with fine spikes, and the price paths of rd-base-6k-s3 and rd-base-24k-s3 named above. loop_with_data's arm b264, which gives the plain bed 2.3 times the budget, is queued on the laptop ahead of this screen and has not trained; full_size_loop_pilot's arm fs-b507 is queued on the server and has not trained. No run has trained with a coarse output step beyond the unit tests.

result.note_on_the_base: The base's score files on the laptop read 1.628284 and 1.482467; the record's base line quoted 1.628291 and 1.482439 from an earlier scoring. The paired leads use the score files.

readings.out8: 0.0073 ahead at 6,000 updates and 0.0009 behind at 24,000 [0.0000, 0.0019]: no lead at 24,000, so it earns no server seeds and no full-size arm. The coarse output stays a saving of energy at no cost in bits (output_step_on_trained_weights.json), reported only. Like every early gain on the bed, its 6k lead fades with data.
readings.out8-b75: 0.0016 behind the base at 24,000 updates [0.0007, 0.0025], within the 0.004 allowed: the saving also holds as a way to train. It trains at 76,187 pulses a byte against the base's 116,193 (34% fewer) for 0.0016 bits a byte. By context it gives up near copies (+0.026) and wins far copies (-0.054); new contexts are level.

result.verdict: Reported only (out8 has no lead at 24,000 updates). The coarse output's energy saving holds when trained in (out8-b75 within 0.004): a model may train with a third fewer pulses at almost no cost in bits.
